questions_and_answers.question_text: Which negative is used with cónglái for state verbs? For process verbs?
What difference do bù and méi make with action verbs?
How does cónglái differ grammatically from cóngqián?
What does shuōdào do at the beginning of a sentence?
Write the Chinese for "She has never gotten married."
Write the Chinese for "We were talking about you just now, and here you are!"

answers.answer_text: Wǒmen gāngcái hái shuōdào nǐ, nǐ jiù lái le!

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which of cónglái méi and cóngqián méi makes the stronger statement?
Write the Chinese for "He will be going abroad soon."
Write the Chinese for "This person is fastidious about what he eats and what he wears."

answers.answer_text: Zhèige rén hěn jiǎng chī, hěn jiǎng chuān.

articles.text:
8. A: Zhōngguo rén cónglái bù jiǎng Didn't the Chinese ever stress equality
      nánnǚ píngděng ma?             between men and women?
   B: Shuōdào nánnǚ píngděng, nà    As for equality of the sexes, that's a
      shi zuìjìn jǐshíniánde xīn     new concept of the last few decades.
      guānniàn.

Notes on No. 8

cónglái bù: "never, never does...." Whether you choose cónglái bù or cónglái méi depends on WHAT KIND OF VERB you are using:

STATE VERBS (use bù):
Wǒde qián cónglái dōu bú gòu.    I have never had enough money.
Wǒ cónglái bù xǐhuan qù Niǔ Yuē. I never like going to New York.

PROCESS VERBS (use méi):
Tā cónglái méi jiéguo hūn.       She has never gotten married.
Tā cónglái méi bìngguo.          He has never gotten sick.

ACTION VERBS (bù and méi make a DIFFERENCE IN MEANING):
Wǒ cónglái méi kànguo zhèiyàngrde I have never read a book like this.
shū.                             (PAST EXPERIENCE)
Wǒ cónglái bú kàn zhèiyàngrde    I never read this kind of book.
shū.                             (HABITUAL)

Cónglái vs. cóngqián: Cóngqián, "the past," is a NOUN, a time word. It may be the object of the prepositional verb zài. Cónglái is NOT a noun; it is used ADVERBIALLY, always between the subject and the verb. Both may sometimes be translated "never," but cónglái méi makes a STRONGER statement.

jiǎng: "to be particular about, to stress, to pay attention to."

Zhèige rén hěn jiǎng chī, hěn    This person is fastidious about what he
jiǎng chuān.                     eats and what he wears.

shuōdào: "to speak of; as for." When -dào is used with verbs of speech (shuō, tán, jiǎng), they are translated as "to speak of" or "to talk about."

Wǒmen gāngcái hái shuōdào nǐ,    We were talking about you just now, and
nǐ jiù lái le!                   here you are!

In sentence 8B, shuōdào is used at the BEGINNING of the sentence to INTRODUCE A TOPIC, as we use "when it comes to" or "speaking of" in English.

Shuōdào jiéhūnde shì, wǒ hái     When it comes to the marriage, I have
děi xiǎngyixiǎng.                to think it over some more.
Tándào Zhōngguo wénhuà, tā bǐ    When it comes to Chinese culture, he
wǒ zhīdaode duō.                 knows a lot more than I do.

zuìjìn: "recently, lately; recent, last." Zuìjìn may be used as a TIME WORD, or as an ADJECTIVE modifying a Number-Counter-Noun. Besides referring to the near past, zuìjìn can also refer to the NEAR FUTURE — "soon."

Tā zuìjìn yào chū guó.           He will be going abroad soon.
